title: Your Right to Information
tagline: How to ask public offices for the information you need.
description: Since 2024, Zambia's Access to Information Act gives everyone a legal way to ask public bodies for information: about a budget, a project, a decision or a service. This course explains what you can ask for, how to make a request step by step, the time limits offices must follow, and what to do if they refuse.
outcomes: Explain what the Access to Information Act, 2023 does
Know what information you can ask for, and what may be withheld
Make a request in writing or orally
Know the time limits for a response
Appeal to the Human Rights Commission if refused
Use information to solve community problems

modules.title: Your right to know
modules.summary: The law, what you can ask for, and what offices must publish.

lessons.title: What is the right to information?
lessons.body:
Public bodies hold a lot of information that affects your life: budgets, plans, contracts, reports and decisions. The **right to information** means you can ask to see it.

## The law
The **Access to Information Act, No. 24 of 2023** was passed in December 2023 and came into force on **25 June 2024**. It supports the freedom of expression in the **Constitution**, which includes the freedom to receive information.

## Who must give information
The Act applies to **information holders**. These are mainly public bodies, such as:

- ministries and government departments,
- councils,
- public institutions and state-owned companies,
- other bodies that use public money or provide public services, as set out in the Act.

They must appoint **information officers** to help people who make requests.

## Who oversees it
The **Human Rights Commission** oversees the Act. It promotes the right to information, and hears **appeals** when people are refused.

## Why it matters
Information helps you:

- check whether a promised project was funded,
- understand why a decision was made,
- find out what services you are entitled to,
- hold leaders accountable with facts instead of rumours.

## You do not need to explain why
In general, you do not have to be a journalist or a lawyer to ask. Any person can make a request. Clear, specific requests get the best results.
key_points: The Access to Information Act, 2023 came into force in June 2024
Public bodies must answer requests
The Human Rights Commission oversees the law
lessons.try_it: Think of one piece of information about your community you would like to know.

lessons.title: Information you can ask for
lessons.body:
You can ask for information that a public body **already holds**, in records such as documents, reports, letters, emails, maps, photos and data.

## Examples of useful requests
- The **budget** and spending for a CDF project in your ward.
- The **contract** and completion date for a road or school project.
- The **minutes** of a council meeting.
- The **criteria** for choosing who receives bursaries or social cash transfer.
- **Inspection reports** for a market, school or clinic.
- **Plans** for land use or a new development in your area.

## Information that may be withheld
The right is not unlimited. The Act allows some information to be withheld or delayed, for example to protect:

- **other people's private information**,
- **safety and security**,
- some **commercial secrets** of businesses,
- matters before the **courts**.

If a request is refused, the office must explain why in writing and tell you that you can appeal.

## Your own information
To see personal information an organisation holds about **you**, such as your records, you can also use your rights under the **Data Protection Act, 2021**.

## Ask for what exists
The Act gives access to existing records. It does not require an office to write a new report or answer opinion questions. Instead of *"Why is the clinic so bad?"* ask *"Please provide the clinic's drug supply records for the last three months."*
key_points: You can ask for records a public body already holds
Some information may be withheld, with written reasons
Ask for specific records, not opinions
lessons.try_it: Rewrite a complaint you have as a request for a specific record.

lessons.title: Information offices must publish
lessons.body:
You do not always need to make a request. The Act also requires information holders to **publish** important information on their own, so the public can find it easily. This is called **proactive disclosure**.

## What this means
Public bodies are expected to make available information of public interest, such as:

- what the body does and how it is organised,
- the services it provides and how to access them,
- its budgets and key reports,
- the contact details of its **information officer**.

Information holders were given time, until June 2026, to put their systems in place.

## Where to look first
Before making a request, check:

- the body's **official website** and Facebook page,
- **notice boards** at councils, schools and clinics,
- **Parliament's** website for budgets, reports and debates,
- the **Auditor General's** reports,
- the **Government Gazette** and **ZambiaLII** for laws.

If the information is already published, you will get it faster.

## Information officers
Every information holder should have an **information officer** whose job is to help you. Ask at the reception of a ministry, council or public body: *"Who is your information officer?"*

## Accessible formats
If you have a disability, you can ask for information in an accessible format, such as large print or read aloud.
key_points: Many offices must publish key information without being asked
Check websites and notice boards first
Ask for the information officer

modules.title: Making a request
modules.summary: Forms, timelines and tips for good requests.

lessons.title: Making a request step by step
lessons.body:
## The form
Requests are made using **Form 1**, set out in the **Access to Information (General) Regulations, 2025**. Ask the information officer for the form, or look for it on the Human Rights Commission's website.

## In writing or by speaking
- You can apply **in writing**, filling in the form.
- You can apply **orally**, by speaking. If you cannot write, the information holder must fill in the form for you.

## The steps
1. Go to the office that holds the information, and ask for the **information officer**.
2. Fill in **three copies** of Form 1.
3. Describe the information clearly: what, which place, which dates.
4. Say what **format** you want, such as a photocopy, an electronic copy, or to view it in person.
5. The office must **date-stamp and sign** the copies. **Keep one copy** as your proof.

## Fees
There may be fees, such as for copying. The office must tell you about any fees **before** it continues processing your request.

## An example description
*"Copies of the bill of quantities, contract and payment records for the 1x3 classroom block at Chawama Primary School, funded by CDF in 2025."*

## Keep a record
Write down the date you submitted, the name of the person who received it, and any reference number. You will need these if there is a delay or refusal.
key_points: Use Form 1, in writing or orally
Fill three copies and keep a stamped one
Fees must be told to you in advance
lessons.try_it: Write a one-sentence description of information you would request, with place and dates.

lessons.title: Time limits: how long they have
lessons.body:
The law sets clear **time limits**, so requests cannot be ignored forever.

## The main deadlines
- **7 days:** the information holder must decide whether to give you the information and tell you **in writing**.
- If another body holds the information, your request may be **transferred** within **5 days**, and you must be told within **7 days**.
- The holder can **extend** the time by up to **14 days**, but must give you written reasons within 7 days.
- If information is going to be published soon, access may be **deferred**, normally for no more than **30 days**. You can respond with your reasons within **14 days**.

## If they do not answer
If the information holder does not respond within the time allowed, the request is **treated as refused**. This is called a **deemed refusal**. You can then appeal.

## If the information cannot be found
If a record cannot be found after a reasonable search, the holder must tell you in writing. If it is found later, they must process your request within **7 days**.

## Keep track
Mark the dates on a calendar from the day your copy was stamped. If a deadline passes, follow up politely with your reference number before appealing.

## Days and details
The exact rules are in the Act and the 2025 Regulations. The Human Rights Commission publishes guides that explain them.
key_points: 7 days for a written decision
Extensions of up to 14 days need written reasons
No answer in time counts as a refusal you can appeal
lessons.try_it: Mark on a calendar what date would be 7 days from today.

lessons.title: Tips for a request that works
lessons.body:
A well-written request is easier to answer and harder to refuse.

## Be specific
- Name the **place**: the school, ward, road or market.
- Give **dates** or periods: *January to June 2026*.
- Name the **type of record**: contract, minutes, budget, report.

## Ask for a little at a time
A request for *"all documents about roads"* may be slow or refused as too large. Start with one project or one document.

## Use the right office
Send the request to the body that holds the information. For a CDF project, start with the **council**. For a national programme, the **ministry**.

## Be polite and patient
Officers are more willing to help when treated with respect. Many requests are answered smoothly.

## Work together
Community groups, parent-teacher associations and residents' groups can make requests together. Sharing the work also shares the results.

## Use what you receive
When you get information:

- read it carefully and compare it with what you see on the ground,
- keep the original safe,
- share it accurately, without adding claims you cannot prove.

## Protect yourself
Requests are a lawful right. If anyone threatens you for making a request, keep evidence and report it to the Human Rights Commission or the police.
key_points: Be specific about place, dates and type of record
Ask for one thing at a time
Requests are your lawful right
lessons.try_it: Improve this request: 'Give me road documents.'

modules.title: When things go wrong
modules.summary: Refusals, appeals and using information well.

lessons.title: Practice: if they say no
lessons.body:
*You asked the council for the payment records of a CDF borehole project. After 7 days, you get a letter that says only: "Request refused."*

## Step 1: Check the letter
A refusal must be **in writing**, give **reasons**, name the **part of the law** relied on, and tell you that you can **appeal**. This letter does none of these.

## Step 2: Ask politely
Go back to the information officer with your stamped copy. Say:

*"Thank you for your reply. Under the Access to Information Act, a refusal should give reasons and the legal provision relied on. Could you please provide these?"*

Sometimes the refusal was a misunderstanding, and asking clearly solves it.

## Step 3: Consider narrowing the request
If the office says the request is too broad, or includes private information about individuals, offer to accept part of the information, such as totals, with personal details removed.

## Step 4: Appeal
If you are still refused, you can **appeal to the Human Rights Commission**. The next lesson explains how.

## Keep everything
Keep your stamped request, the refusal letter, notes of conversations with dates and names, and any other replies. These are your evidence for the appeal.

## Stay calm
A refusal is not the end. Many people get information after asking again politely or appealing.
key_points: Refusals must be in writing with reasons
Ask for the reasons and legal provision
Keep all papers for an appeal
lessons.try_it: Practise what you would say to an information officer who refused without reasons.

lessons.title: Appealing to the Human Rights Commission
lessons.body:
If your request is refused, delayed beyond the time limits, or not answered, you can **appeal** to the **Human Rights Commission (HRC)**.

## When you can appeal
- Your request was **refused**, fully or partly.
- The holder **extended** the time and you disagree.
- There was **no response** in time (a deemed refusal).

Appeal against a decision within **30 days** of receiving it.

## How to appeal
Contact the Human Rights Commission. You can:

- visit **Human Rights House** on Independence Avenue in Lusaka,
- call the **toll-free line 8181**,
- email **complaints@hrc.org.zm**,
- visit **www.hrc.org.zm** for forms and guides.

## What to include
- Your name and contact details.
- The information holder and the information you asked for.
- The date of your request (your stamped copy).
- What happened: the refusal letter, or that no answer came.
- What you want: the information released.

## What happens next
The Commission considers the appeal and, after any hearing, must decide within **30 days** of concluding it. It can order the information to be released.

## It is free to ask
Contacting the Human Rights Commission does not require a lawyer. Bring your papers and explain clearly.
key_points: Appeal to the Human Rights Commission within 30 days
HRC toll-free line: 8181
Bring your stamped request and the refusal
lessons.try_it: Save the HRC toll-free number, 8181, in your contacts.

lessons.title: Using information to make change
lessons.body:
Information on its own does not fix a borehole. Using it well does.

## Compare paper with reality
Compare what the records say with what you see. *The contract says the borehole was completed in March, but there is no borehole.* That is a powerful, factual finding.

## Share responsibly
- Share the **facts** and the **documents**, not rumours.
- Separate what you **know** from what you **suspect**.
- Do not share people's private information.

## Take it to the right people
- **Your councillor** and **Ward Development Committee**.
- **The council's** officers, and your **MP**.
- **Community meetings** and **local radio** call-in programmes.
- The **Anti-Corruption Commission** if there are signs of corruption.

## Work with others
Parent-teacher associations, church groups, residents' associations and civil society organisations can add weight. A group that brings documents and photos to a meeting is hard to ignore.

## Follow up and celebrate
Keep asking until the problem is fixed. When it is, share that too. Success encourages others to use their right to information.

## Respect and safety
Be respectful even when you are frustrated. Facts presented calmly persuade more people, and protect you from claims that you are spreading lies.
key_points: Compare records with what you see
Share facts and documents, not rumours
Take findings to the right people and follow up
